questions.question_text: Alterations in which area(s) of the brain are most highly associated with known deficits for suicidal individuals?

options.text: The somatosensory cortex and the corpus callosum

questions.explanation: Postmortem studies in adolescents who completed suicide have demonstrated the greatest degree of alteration in the prefrontal cortex and hippocampus, areas associated with known deficits for suicidal individuals, namely emotion regulation and problem solving[cite: 8]. These studies have shown alteration in 5-HT2A binding, decreased activity of protein kinase A and C, downregulation in cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) response element–binding (CREB) protein, and increased activity of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), which are involved in signaling and protection from the neurotoxic effects of stress[cite: 8].

questions.question_text: True statements about the phenomenology of bipolar disorder in children and adolescents include all of the following except

options.text: Prepubertal children very rarely exhibit discrete episodes of mania or depression.

Some clinicians ascribe symptoms such as extreme mood variability, aggressive behavior, and high rates of distractibility and impulsivity to pediatric bipolar disorder, although controversy exists over this diagnosis.
Psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusional thought content are rare in adolescent mania.
Among adolescents, depressive episodes characterized by severely depressed mood, psychosis, psychomotor retardation, and hypersomnia may be predictive of later development of bipolar disorder.
Antidepressant medications may trigger hypomania or mania in children and adolescents with no known history of bipolar disorder.

correct_answer.text: Psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusional thought content are rare in adolescent mania.

correct_answers.text: Psychotic symptoms such as hallucinations and delusional thought content are rare in adolescent mania.

questions.explanation: Bipolar disorder is being diagnosed with increasing frequency in prepubertal children even though in this age group, “classic” manic episodes are extremely rare, and prepubertal children very infrequently exhibit discrete episodes of mania or depression[cite: 8]. Although an ongoing controversy exists over the diagnosis of bipolar disorder in this age group, increasing numbers of clinicians diagnose bipolar disorder based on findings of extreme mood variability, aggression, distractibility, impulsivity, and depressive symptoms, particularly in the context of a family history of bipolar disorder[cite: 8]. Whether these children will go on to develop more discrete mood cycling later as they mature or whether their presentations will differ from adult bipolar disorder remains under investigation[cite: 8]. Adolescent-onset bipolar disorder much more closely parallels in its presentation the characteristics of bipolar disorder in adults[cite: 8]. Psychotic symptoms, such as hallucinations and delusions, are common (not rare) in adolescent mania; indeed, some authors suggest that psychosis as part of a manic state is more common in adolescents than in adults[cite: 8]. Adolescents with depressive episodes characterized by severely depressed mood, psychosis, psychomotor retardation, and hypersomnia may be at increased risk of going on to develop bipolar disorder compared with adolescents whose major depressive episodes are not so characterized[cite: 8]. As in adults, antidepressant medications may trigger hypomania or mania in children and adolescents with no known history of bipolar disorder[cite: 8].

questions.question_text: Major depressive disorder in school-aged children

options.text: may present as irritable mood rather than depressed mood
includes mood-congruent auditory hallucinations less commonly than in adults with the same disorder
is never diagnosed in the context of bereavement

correct_answer.text: may present as irritable mood rather than depressed mood

correct_answers.text: may present as irritable mood rather than depressed mood

questions.explanation: Major depression in school-aged children does not commonly present with findings typical among adults, such as depressed mood and neurovegetative symptoms; instead, somatic complaints, psychomotor agitation, and irritable mood are more common[cite: 8]. Additionally, mood-congruent auditory hallucinations are much more (not less) common among prepubertal children with major depression than among adults with the same condition[cite: 8]. Pervasive anhedonia, a common finding in depressed adults, is less typical (not usually present) among school-aged children with major depression[cite: 8]. A diagnosis of major depressive disorder is not usually made within 2 months of the loss of a loved one; however, in the event of marked functional impairment, morbid preoccupation with worthlessness or guilt, psychomotor retardation, suicidal ideation, or psychosis, a diagnosis of major depression and appropriate treatment are indicated[cite: 8].

questions.question_text: Approximately what percent of adolescent suicide victims had a mood disorder at the time of their death?
questions.explanation: Mood disorders are strongly associated with suicidal ideation, attempts, and completions[cite: 8]. Approximately 60 percent of adolescent suicide victims had a mood disorder at the time of death[cite: 8]. Bipolar disorder appears to convey a particularly high risk for suicidal attempts and completions, particularly at times when patients are experiencing rapid cycling or a mixed state, both of which are more common conditions in pediatric than in adult bipolar disorder[cite: 8]. One study found that nearly 20 percent of adolescent suicide victims had bipolar spectrum disorder, although other studies did not[cite: 8]. The rate of suicidal behavior in clinical samples of pediatric bipolar disorder is quite high, with around one-third reporting a lifetime history of suicide attempt[cite: 8]. Among the symptoms of depression most closely associated with suicidal ideation and behavior are insomnia, agitation, and irritability[cite: 8].

questions.question_text: Which is the only medication that has been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of depression in children?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine (Prozac) is the only medication to have FDA approval for the treatment of major depression in children and adolescents[cite: 8]. In two double-blind, placebo-controlled trials, significantly more of the patients treated with fluoxetine were much or very much improved (56 and 52 percent, respectively) than the placebo group (33 and 37 percent, respectively)[cite: 8]. Fluoxetine alone, fluoxetine with cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), CBT alone, and placebo were compared in a large multicenter trial of 439 adolescent outpatients with major depression[cite: 8]. Significantly more of the fluoxetine-treated patients were much or very much improved compared with the placebo group[cite: 8]. The combination of fluoxetine plus CBT had the highest response rate[cite: 8]. Remission rates were also significantly higher in the combination group than in the fluoxetine, CBT, and placebo groups[cite: 8]. Predictors of treatment response included a younger age, higher functioning, less chronicity, less suicidal ideation, less hopelessness, fewer comorbidities, and higher expectation for improvement[cite: 8].

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms presents with similar frequency among children, adolescents, and adults with major depressive disorder?
questions.explanation: Although the core symptoms of major depressive disorder overlap considerably among children, adolescents, and adults, different symptoms predominate in each age group[cite: 8]. Suicidal ideation is a symptom that occurs with similar frequency among depressed individuals of all ages[cite: 8]. Psychomotor agitation, irritable mood, somatic complaints, and mood-congruent auditory hallucinations are common manifestations of major depression among school-age children[cite: 8]. Pervasive anhedonia is less common among children but is frequently present in depressed adolescents and adults[cite: 8]. Adolescents with depression also present more commonly with irritability, aggression, sulkiness, withdrawal from social activities, and a desire to leave home than do depressed patients from other age groups[cite: 8]. Changes in sleep and appetite are more common in adults with major depression than in children or adolescents with the disorder[cite: 8].

questions.question_text: Which of the following treatments have demonstrated efficacy in treating adolescent depression based on controlled clinical trials?
questions.explanation: A number of studies have demonstrated the efficacy of cognitive-behavioral psychotherapy in treating major depressive disorder in adolescents[cite: 8]. Interpersonal therapy has also shown good resultsin the treatment of depressed adolescents[cite: 8]. Recent controversies surrounding potential side effects of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors among children and adolescents, including the possible increase in suicidal ideation, have complicated the use of these medications to treat adolescents with major depressive disorder; nevertheless, fluoxetine has been to shown to effectively treat the condition in this age group[cite: 8].
